question: What does the pronoun in إنها refer to?

positions.position: Saqar, Hell, or the Fire.
positions.reasons: Al-Farra, al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur connect the pronoun to the previously named Saqar (Ibn Ashur cites 74:26); Qatada, Mujahid, Abu Razin, Ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak and Ibn Abbas identify it as Fire or Hell. Abu Hayyan prefers this as the apparent antecedent; al-Tabataba'i reports it as the usual view. Ibn al-Jawzi transmits Hasan's remark that nothing warned of is frailer than Saqar.

positions.position: The warning.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya proposes this alongside the affair of the afterlife; Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi also report it as an alternative antecedent.

positions.position: The affair of the afterlife.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya compares 38:67; Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi report this alternative.

positions.position: The Resurrection or rising of the Hour.
positions.reasons: Al-Mawardi calls it one of the great calamities and punishments; al-Qurtubi transmits this from Ibn Abbas. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi note that the antecedent is unstated; al-Samin adds an objection about gender.

positions.position: The denial of Muhammad's prophethood, a grave sin.
positions.reasons: Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi report Ibn Abbas; Study Quran reports the same alternative through Q and Ṭ and again through Q.

positions.position: The Quran, one of God's greatest signs and a universal warning.
positions.reasons: Al-Tabataba'i prefers this because the rebuke answers the accusation that the Quran is magic or human speech; its warning releases followers from deeds binding them to Saqar. Al-Tabrisi offers Quranic warnings as the alternative to Saqar.

positions.position: This verse, one of the great signs.
positions.reasons: Al-Mawardi reports Ibn Isa's proposal.

positions.position: A pronoun of the matter, with no specific antecedent.
positions.reasons: Al-Samin lists this grammatical possibility.

turns_on: Whether an antecedent is the named Saqar, a warning or afterlife event, the Quran or verse under attack, or an implicit matter; the Resurrection proposal faces unstated-antecedent and gender objections.

question: How is the hamza of لإحدى read and explained?

positions.position: The hamza is fully pronounced and retained in connected speech.
positions.reasons: Al-Farisi reports Qunbul from Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr with hamza; Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Samin call this the common reading. Al-Wahidi and al-Razi call its alif hamzat qatʿ, retained in connection.

positions.position: The hamza is omitted: la-hda.
positions.reasons: A report from Ibn Kathir is given by al-Farisi, al-Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, al-Tabrisi, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi; Ibn Atiyya and al-Samin add Nasr ibn Asim; Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi add Ibn Muhaysin, and Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi name Wahb ibn Jarir's report from Ibn Kathir. Al-Wahidi cites Abu al-Aswad, Ahmad ibn Yahya and al-Farazdaq's poetry; al-Farisi cites al-Farazdaq's إثم and 6:74, 14:35, 43:26, and 22:58. Ibn Atiyya and al-Tabrisi cite Abu al-Aswad and Thaʿlab; al-Tabrisi gives Abu al-Aswad's address to Ziyad, 'father of al-Mughira,' and al-Farazdaq's line on Atiyya's sin. Al-Farisi and al-Wahidi object that deletion is non-analogical and leaves an initial consonant cluster, but the attached lam makes deletion word-internal; al-Wahidi compares lahu and ʿuḍudan. Al-Samin proposes hamza to alif followed by loss of alif when two vowelless letters meet. Al-Alusi calls the deletion light but irregular; al-Samin says it cannot found a productive analogy. Al-Razi compares waylamma.

positions.position: The hamza is eased to an intermediate sound between hamza and vowel.
positions.reasons: Al-Farisi, al-Wahidi, Abu Ali as reported by Ibn Atiyya, al-Tabrisi, al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin say this is the regular analogical easing, in contrast to complete omission.

turns_on: The transmitted pronunciation and whether ordinary hamza easing licenses complete deletion after the attached lam.

question: How is the feminine form إحدى built?

positions.position: It is an original feminine formation rather than a form derived from a masculine base.
positions.reasons: Al-Wahidi compares ʿasa and ukhra.

question: What force does calling it إحدى الكبر have?

positions.position: It is one among many great calamities, with more tribulations implied.
positions.reasons: Al-Alusi reports al-Zamakhshari's reading and prefers it as fitting the context and hinting at further tribulations. Study Quran reports an inference that such calamities will be endless.

positions.position: It is uniquely prominent among the greatest, unequalled in magnitude.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur says the sentence works like a proverb, comparing an outstanding man among notable men and إحدى حظيات لقمان, and refers to 74:11. Al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan stress that its greatness is without equal; Bursevi gives this nuance if the expression is understood as definite. Al-Alusi reports a reading of unique greatness alongside al-Zamakhshari's alternative.

turns_on: Whether 'one of' counts an item among many great calamities or is an idiom for singular prominence.

question: What is the singular and formation of الكبر?

positions.position: It is the plural of كبرى, a feminine form.
positions.reasons: Ibn Qutayba compares ūlā/awwal and sughrā/sughr; al-Wahidi compares sughrā/sughar; al-Jishumi adds ukhrā/ukhar; Ibn al-Jawzi compares ṣighar/ṣughrā; al-Qurtubi adds ʿuẓmā/ʿuẓam and says the feminine is built directly, not from a masculine base. Al-Kashshaf, reported by al-Razi, treats the feminine ending like tāʾ marbūṭa and compares plurals for dust and a burrowing animal. Al-Baydawi says the plural follows an analogy to its verb; Abu Hayyan says the feminine alif drops. Ibn Ashur calls it an irregular broken plural that treats kubrā as a noun for a calamity rather than an adjective, unlike ʿuẓmā. Al-Tabrisi, al-Nahhas and others gloss the plural as great matters.

positions.position: It is the plural of كبيرة.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya states this. Abu Hayyan and al-Samin suspect a copyist's error; al-Alusi calls the claim mistaken.

turns_on: Whether the attested plural is formed from kubrā or kabīra; three later authors reject or suspect a copying error in the latter attribution.

question: What are the الكبر counted here?

positions.position: Great calamities, disasters, horrors, or severe punishments.
positions.reasons: Ibn Qutayba and al-Mubarrad gloss the expression as one of the disasters; al-Qurtubi cites a rajaz line for kubar as a major calamity, Abu Hayyan cites another rajaz line for devastating misfortune, and al-Samin cites Ibn al-Muʿalla's verse. Al-Wahidi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, al-Samin and others apply this sense to Hell. Al-Farra's analysis connects the next verse's nadhīran to 'one of the great calamities.'

positions.position: The seven gates or levels of Hell, with Saqar one of them.
positions.reasons: Muqatil, al-Kalbi and Ibn al-Sa'ib are transmitted as listing Jahannam, Laza, Hutama, Saʿir, Saqar, Jahim and Hawiya; al-Biqa'i repeats the seven names. Al-Razi and al-Alusi report the interpretation. Al-Alusi says the seven-level account is unpersuasive.

positions.position: A name of Hell.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurtubi reports Muqatil's use of al-kubar as one of Hell's names.

positions.position: Great divine signs, including the Quranic warning or Saqar as proof of power.
positions.reasons: Al-Mawardi reports Ibn Isa's verse-as-sign interpretation; al-Tabrisi offers the Quran's warnings as signs; al-Tabataba'i calls the Quran one of God's greatest signs. Bursevi says Saqar is a great sign if the objection concerns signs, or proof that God subdues sinners from Adam to the Resurrection with only a few guards if it concerns their number.

turns_on: Whether the plural names calamities or punishments, Hell's seven divisions, Hell itself, or divine signs; the proposed antecedent and surrounding dispute affect the choice.

question: What grammatical constraint governs the feminine superlative in الكبر?

positions.position: A feminine فعلى superlative is used with من, in a construct, or with the definite article.
positions.reasons: Al-Burhan compares its restriction with that of afʿal and cites definite feminine forms; al-Nahhas says al-kubar retains the article and so is diptote.

question: How does this clause relate to the oath and the preceding كلا?

positions.position: The clause answers the oath by the moon, night, and dawn.
positions.reasons: Al-Tabrisi identifies Saqar's greatness as the oath's answer; al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur take it as the apparent or straightforward syntax; al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Alusi and al-Tabataba'i report it. Ibn Ashur says the oath begins a new statement about Saqar, citing 74:26 and 74:31. Islahi says the Quranic warning verses complete the oaths by portraying Hell as a grave upheaval rather than a jest.

positions.position: It explains the rebuke كلا; the intervening oath emphasizes the rebuke or has an implicit answer.
positions.reasons: Al-Razi, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Tabataba'i report this analysis, associated with al-Zamakhshari; al-Samin rejects it as forced and contrary to apparent syntax. Al-Alusi says kalla rebukes a denier and the oath is parenthetical or has an implied answer. Ibn Ashur says the oath can conclude rejection of the claim about Hell's guards (74:26), with this clause explaining that rejection. Al-Tabataba'i notes another possible function for kalla beyond two readings without specifying it in this note.

positions.position: The earlier كلا rejects the preceding claim about the parable; intervening material is parenthetical and the oath starts a new statement.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur says this permits a pause after kalla. He describes kalla as a rebuke and rejection of a claim, citing 26:61–62 and 19:77.

turns_on: Where the oath's answer is placed and whether كلا begins a rebuke explained by the clause; al-Samin objects that the parenthetical analysis strains the apparent syntax.

question: How is the following نذيرا للبشر connected grammatically to this clause?

positions.position: نذيرا is accusative, linked to 'one of the great calamities' as an indefinite after a definite expression or as a warning verbal noun.
positions.reasons: Al-Farra prefers this attachment and offers the two grammatical analyses.

positions.position: نذيرٌ للبشر is nominative singular, 'a warner to humankind.'
positions.reasons: Al-Farra reports Ubayy's reading and says both readings are sound.

turns_on: Whether the following warning is an accusative associated with this clause or a nominative singular in Ubayy's reading.

question: What do the nearby warning and oath signs teach?

positions.position: The Quran warns humanity of Hell and the Hereafter so people may prepare and escape its consequences.
positions.reasons: Al-Tabataba'i says the Quran clears the accusation against it and frees followers from deeds tying them to Saqar. Islahi says natural manifestations argue for the Hereafter and expose heedlessness; those evading the Quran's warning retreat into stubbornness. His other note says Hell's warning is a grave upheaval, not a jest, and mockers are unfortunate. Kuran Yolu says the oaths draw attention to divine signs and the warning's importance.

positions.position: The moon, departing night and brightening dawn point to divine power and the passage from darkness or disbelief to light and guidance.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur says three oath clauses give conventional threefold emphasis and invoke a great created object and two signs of God's power. Their light in darkness evokes guidance, misguidance and Quranic light. Night departs as dawn brightens; the adverbs إذ and إذا are circumstantial, and the sequence recalls Islam removing disbelief, as at 14:1. Kuran Yolu likewise sees divine signs in the oaths.

turns_on: Whether the note explains the Quranic warning's aim or the imagery and emphatic force of the three oaths.

question: What do the two readings of the preceding night-oath say?

positions.position: إذ أدبر uses إذ with a past-tense form, swearing by the recurring moment when night has departed.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur attributes it to Nafi, Hamza, Hafs, Yaqub and Khalaf.

positions.position: إذا دبر uses the future-time adverb and a plain verb meaning departed, parallel to إذا أسفر.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur attributes it to Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, Abu Amr, Abu Bakr from Asim, al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far; he says both readings are sound.

turns_on: The time adverb and verb form for the night’s departure; Ibn Ashur regards both as sound.

question: How do inward readings understand the great warning?

positions.position: It warns against a return to injustice or inward darkness after illumination.
positions.reasons: Al-Sulami says warning to humanity confirms the matter for those granted direct illumination; al-Qushayri fears darkness returning to hearts after reality is disclosed.

positions.position: Prophetic warning returns those absorbed in conformity to spiritual witnessing, though conformity has no significance at direct vision.
positions.reasons: Al-Sulami reports al-Wasiti: lights appear to the spirits of the unifiers, and warning calls them back to their witness.

positions.position: Saqar signifies nature or the lower self's hell; its warning benefits receptive souls who can rise toward heart and spirit.
positions.reasons: Al-Qashani contrasts receptive people who attain virtues with others descending into bodily desire. Bursevi connects the hell of the lower self to the preceding moon, night and dawn imagery.

turns_on: Whether the spiritual danger is renewed injustice and darkness, unreflective conformity, or descent into nature and bodily desire.

question: What other rhetorical effects are noted around this verse?

positions.position: Repetition lends emphasis.
positions.reasons: Abu Ubayda illustrates this with repeated 'I saw,' awlā laka, three plus seven restated as ten, and the reiterated curse of Abu Lahab.

positions.position: The two occurrences of البشر form complete paronomasia.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur compares the occurrence in the passage with لواحة للبشر at 74:29.

positions.position: Rhetorical merit comes from a phrase's arrangement and the extra nuance it conveys.
positions.reasons: Al-Jurjani compares كأن زيدا الأسد with زيد كالأسد: the former makes Zayd's bravery seem indistinguishable from a lion's.

turns_on: The notes identify separate rhetorical devices in the surrounding discussion: emphasis, paronomasia, and added nuance from arrangement.
